## Monitoring methods {#sec-monitoring-methods}

### Overview over available methods

The supporting EU document Guidance on establishing surveillance systems for invasive alien species of Union concern in terrestrial and freshwater environments (ref) lists the following monitoring methods for the monitoring of chinese muntjac:

-   acoustic surveys\
-   camera traps and drones\
-   citizen science\
-   surveys for tracks and signs\
-   trapping, netting, and collecting\
-   visual surveys

In the expert survey on the situation of Union list (candidate) IAS in Flanders conducted by INBO (ref),

-   camera traps and\
-   visual surveys (including tracks and signs and the use of infrared devices)

were also reported as potential methods.
In addition,

-   passive acoustic monitoring, and\
-   airborne environmental DNA

were mentioned, but it was remarked that these methods either require more research or are inferior to others.
When asked which method was the most relevant, the expert clearly indicated camera traps.

In what follows, we provide descriptions of all above listed methods.
We start with the most relevant method, camera traps.
Here we present a relatively detailed account while we keep information more concise for the remaining techniques.

### Camera traps

The following description is based on Bollen et al. (ref) and the IUCN guidance document for surveillance schemes (pp. 35 - 43; ref)..

Camera traps are **devices that use sensors and digital cameras to automatically record images of passing wildlife**.
The technique is well-suited to monitor medium-sized to large, warm-blooded and terrestrial animal species.

Sensors can be infrared-based, detecting changes in the temperature profile within the measurement range, or triggered by motion.
Cameras can take still images or videos, and record during the day as well as at night.
Images can be stored on a medium for later examination, or be transmitted in real time.
Processing of camera trap images is aided by specialised software and automatic classification by means of machine learning algorithms, although manual processing currently remains an important component.

Traps are mainly used in terrestrial environments, where they can be attached to trees.
Their performance can be improved with the strategic use of baits or lures.
Camera traps per se do not track individual animals, and individual identification requires marking animals.

#### Technical parameters

On a more detailed level, the following technical parameters require attention (recommendations are taken from Bollen et al. (ref)):

-   **Trigger type**: whether the camera is triggered in an active or passive way; passive triggering is currently the standard and well-suited for not too small mammal species such as the Chinese muntjac; the associated sensor should be infrared-based if pictures are to taken during times of reduced daylight
-   **Trigger speed**: speed at which the camera takes a photo after detection; should be very fast, i.e., at least \< 1 s and preferably \< 0.6 s
-   **Recovery time**: time between two subsequent camera activations; should also be as fast as possible, as an image series (see next point) of the same group of animals facilitates the determination of e.g. the species
-   **Burst mode**: upon activation, a series of images of e.g. 10 images is taken instead of a single image; highly recommended and preferred above video mode, which usually comes with slower trigger speeds and longer recovery times, and consumes more electricity
-   **Detection zone**: zone in front of the camera in which animals are detected; has the shape of a circular segment and as such is determined by a detection distance and a detection angle; the detection distance - the radius of the circular segment - is the maximum distance from the camera at which an animal can be detected; the detection angle is the maximum angle within which animals are detected relative to the camera's viewing direction; both should be as large as possible, especially for rare and/or difficult-to-detect species, such as the Chinese muntjac
-   **Flash**: an invisible infrared fash causes minimal interference but also black-and white images only; white flash in case images should be in color to aid identification of individual animals; disturbing, however
-   **Batteries**: especially battery running time and battery life expectancy should be considered.
-   **Camera cases**: cases should ideally be compact, lightweight, water-resistant, and sturdy to protect the camera from impact; a cable lock for attaching cameras to e.g. trees is recommended to mitigate theft.
-   **Programmable operation schedules**: If photos are to be taken at specific times (e.g., only at night), then cameras should be programmable
-   **Image sensors**: If high-resolution photos are required, for artistic purposes or for identifying individuals, we recommend purchasing full-frame (DSLR) cameras.
-   **Image transfer**: if images should be transferred in real time, the corresponding functionality is required; however, the strength of the network signal (telephony, Wi-Fi) at the location should be considered as a potential bottleneck.
-   **Technical support**: Finally, the reputation of the manufacturer, customer service, technical support and warranty are also considerations when purchasing a camera.

#### Costs

Initial purchase price for the required equipment (cameras, batteries, storage media) can be relatively high.
Depending on the above-discussed technical parameters, camera prices range from 150 to 500 EUR per piece.
Deploying the method involves costs beyond equipment, including staff time for setup, maintenance, data collection, and analysis.
However, staff time is less closely tied to monitoring duration, as compared to other methods such as visual surveys, so camera traps become relatively cost efficient in the long run.
Cameras normally last about five years.

A large-scale monitoring system with 100 cameras may require two months of labor annually for upkeep.
While cameras typically last around five years, 10–30% may need replacement each year due to theft or malfunction.

#### Advantages and disadvantages

In summary, we can distil the following advantage and disadvantages of camera traps:

Advantages:

-   Multiple animal species can in principle be detected simultaneously
-   Minimal human interference
-   Can be used for quasi continuous monitoring
-   Can be used for extended periods of time
-   Maintenance efforts are limited
-   Relatively cost efficient

Disadvantages:

-   Potential technical issues (e.g., battery issues, capacity of storage medium)
-   Potential damaging and theft of cameras
-   Animal sensitivity to camera sounds
-   Elusive species can be hard to detect
-   False activation triggers (e.g., through moving vegetation) consume energy and cause irrelevant images
-   Potential privacy concerns
-   Manual image processing is laborious, but currently still often required as automatic approaches suffer from limited accuracy

### Passive acoustic monitoring

Passive Acoustic Monitoring (PAM) is a non-invasive wildlife monitoring technique that involves recording and analyzing sounds produced by animals or their environment.
It is particularly effective for detecting species that are vocal, cryptic, nocturnal, or difficult to observe directly, such as bats, birds, frogs, marine mammals, and some insects.
PAM relies on devices like autonomous recording units (ARUs) or hydrophones (for underwater monitoring), which can be deployed in remote or hard-to-access areas for extended periods.

This technique allows for continuous, long-term data collection without disturbing wildlife, making it suitable for tracking seasonal activity, migration patterns, population trends, and species presence or absence.
Acoustic data can be analyzed using specialized software to identify species-specific calls, often aided by automated recognition algorithms and call libraries.

While PAM is highly effective, it has limitations.
Data analysis can be time-consuming, especially when call recognition software is unavailable or inaccurate.
Background noise, overlapping calls, and species with similar vocalizations can also pose challenges.
Equipment costs vary but are increasingly affordable, and deployment requires minimal field effort.

#### Suitability for chinese muntjac

Passive acoustic monitoring is an emerging technique for detecting Reeves’ muntjac, capitalizing on their distinctive bark-like vocalizations.
Recent efforts include a UK-based project that trained an artificial intelligence model using recordings collected with Audiomoth recorders over eight weeks; the model was able to identify muntjac calls with a 99.7% success rate, demonstrating strong potential for automated detection.
The IUCN guidance on IAS surveillance (ref) also reports that in areas of high muntjac density, acoustic sensors recorded calls on 60% of nights per sensor, with detection distances of at least 200 meters.
Although muntjac are known to vocalize year-round, they appear to call more frequently at night during the summer months—likely enhancing detectability during this period.
Summer may also be a particularly suitable time for acoustic monitoring, as dense vegetation can limit the effectiveness of camera traps.

### Visual surveys

Visual surveys are a key method for identifying and monitoring invasive alien species (IAS).
They involve recording species with the aid of optical tools (e.g. binoculars, scopes), noting location, date, and recorder, often supplemented with GPS, photographs, or physical samples.
Field identification is preferred, but lab analysis may be needed for verification, especially for difficult species, which may require DNA analysis.

Though labor-intensive and costly, visual surveys are among the most reliable surveillance methods.

Surveys require trained personnel and, where applicable, volunteers.
Costs vary based on habitat, time of year, and equipment (e.g. binoculars, scopes, drones, boats).
A two-person team may survey \~5 km² per day.
Specialized equipment is essential, and aquatic surveys are particularly time-consuming and expensive.
Vehicle-based surveys, especially nocturnal ones, need additional gear like spotlights and night-vision tools.

#### Suitability for chinese muntjac

Visual surveys are a traditional yet generally limited method for detecting Chinese muntjac.
Due to their cryptic behaviour, solitary lifestyle, and predominantly crepuscular to nocturnal activity, visual detection is inherently challenging—especially in the dense vegetation and forest understorey habitats preferred by this species.
As a result, visual surveys tend to yield low and variable detection probabilities and are mostly confined to open areas or periods of high activity.
Hemami et al. (2007) emphasized that even when using technology such as thermal imaging—which greatly improves detection rates—muntjac remain difficult to detect in dense vegetation due to their low stature and hunched posture.
Visual observations, being even more affected by these constraints, are thus best considered opportunistic and inadequate for robust population estimation across heterogeneous landscapes.
While the method is low-cost and straightforward to deploy, its practical utility is restricted to specific contexts such as open habitats or sites known to host high muntjac densities.

### Surveys for tracks and signs

Surveys for tracks and signs are valuable methods for detecting species that are difficult to observe directly.
These indirect approaches rely on identifying physical evidence left by animals, such as droppings, footprints, feeding marks, nests, hairs, and roadkill.
Such signs can indicate the presence or absence of a species in an area, and in some cases, provide an index of local abundance, helping guide management decisions.

Common methods include searching for droppings, which can sometimes be counted to estimate abundance, and examining footprints in natural substrates like mud or in prepared traps such as wet clay trays or sand beds.
Floating rafts and tracking tunnels are effective for aquatic and small terrestrial mammals.
Nest structures (e.g. dreys or dens), feeding damage (e.g. bark stripping), and hairs collected via sticky pads or barbed materials are also used.
Roadkill surveys can supplement data, particularly for elusive or nocturnal species.

These methods are applicable to many mammals on the Union list, but they are species-specific and require trained personnel to interpret results accurately.
Misidentification is a risk, and genetic or microscopic analysis may be necessary for confirmation.
A trained surveyor can typically cover 1 km² per day, with effort and cost depending on habitat complexity and survey intensity.

#### Suitability for chinese muntjac

Surveys for tracks and signs can offer a supplementary means of detecting Chinese muntjac, particularly when direct observations are unlikely due to the species' elusive and crepuscular behaviour.
Signs such as hoofprints, droppings, or evidence of bark stripping and browsing can indicate presence in a given area.
In Flanders, for example, hoofprints have been recorded and used as part of early warning systems (Casaer et al., 2015) .
However, the diagnostic value of such signs can be limited: muntjac tracks are small and may be confused with those of other ungulates, especially roe deer, and their droppings are often not readily distinguishable without detailed inspection.
Furthermore, the detectability of signs is strongly influenced by substrate, weather conditions, and observer skill.
As such, track and sign surveys are considered useful primarily as a confirmatory or supporting tool, rather than a standalone monitoring method.

### Citizen science

Citizen science involves the participation of volunteers in collecting, recording, and sometimes analyzing data in collaboration with scientists.
It is increasingly used in invasive alien species (IAS) monitoring, especially for early detection and expanding geographic coverage.
Volunteers—such as members of the public, hunters, anglers, park visitors, and other stakeholders—can submit observations via apps like iNaturalist or the European Commission’s IAS app, often supported by images or geolocation data.
These contributions are especially valuable in accessible, high-traffic areas like parks and cultural sites.

While citizen science enhances data collection at low cost, species misidentification remains a challenge, particularly for cryptic or look-alike species.
To improve data quality, volunteers should receive training in species identification and sampling procedures.
Initiatives like bioblitzes or tailored campaigns can provide hands-on training, and some volunteers may also assist with sample collection for eDNA analysis.

Technological tools, including image recognition and data-mining from social media, are improving data validation.
However, expert verification and proper coordination remain essential, requiring dedicated staff and resources.
Despite these needs, citizen science remains a cost-effective and scalable method for IAS monitoring, contributing to databases like EASIN and GBIF, and supporting national and EU-wide surveillance and rapid response strategies.

#### Suitability for chinese muntjac

Citizen science can play a supportive role in the early detection and monitoring of Chinese muntjac, particularly in complementing formal surveillance networks.
While the cryptic and predominantly nocturnal behaviour of the species limits the likelihood of frequent visual encounters by members of the public, occasional observations—especially when accompanied by photographs—can still provide valuable signals of presence.
In Belgium, for example, records submitted via platforms such as waarnemingen.be have contributed to early warning systems, and some detections have triggered follow-up action (Casaer et al., 2015; D’hondt et al., 2023).
Citizen scientists who deploy camera traps for general wildlife interest or hunting purposes may also detect muntjac opportunistically, offering a passive yet potentially valuable source of data.

### Airborne environmental DNA

Environmental DNA (eDNA) is a non-invasive technique that detects species by analyzing genetic material they leave in their environment—such as water, soil, or air.
Ideal for monitoring rare or elusive species, it eliminates the need for direct observation or capture.
DNA is shed through faeces, mucus, skin cells, or decomposition and is collected from environmental samples.
These are then processed in laboratories using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with species-specific markers to identify the presence of target species.

Field collection typically requires two people (an expert and a trained assistant or volunteer), though one surveyor may suffice in accessible areas.
Volunteers, such as anglers, can assist with sampling after basic training.
On average, 3–4 sites can be surveyed per day.
Essential sampling equipment includes sterile tubes, gloves, alcohol, and prepaid envelopes for lab submission.

Laboratory processing requires specialist expertise, dedicated facilities, and financial resources.
Costs vary, but DNA analysis typically ranges from €100–200 per sample per species.
Prices decrease with batch processing—for example, down to €50 per sample for 24 samples.
While eDNA offers efficient detection, it has limitations such as false positives/negatives and challenges in estimating abundance.
Nonetheless, it is a valuable tool when integrated with traditional monitoring methods.

#### Suitability for chinese muntjac

Airborne environmental DNA (eDNA) is a novel technique that enables species detection by capturing and sequencing tiny fragments of genetic material shed by organisms into the air.
This approach involves filtering airborne particles onto specialized membranes, which are then analysed for traces of DNA, allowing for non-invasive monitoring of vertebrate presence.
In a proof-of-concept study conducted in a UK zoo setting ([Clare et al., 2022](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S096098222101650X)), Reeves’ muntjac was among the mammal species successfully detected via airborne eDNA sampling.
The study demonstrated that even relatively small and cryptic mammals could be identified with high confidence, highlighting the method’s potential for monitoring elusive terrestrial species without requiring visual contact or physical traces.
However, the approach remains in its early stages, and further research is needed to assess its effectiveness under field conditions, especially in natural habitats where air flow, vegetation, and background DNA may influence detection rates.
